title: Motion graphs; Constant-acceleration equations; Drag and terminal velocity
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: D11-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; K03-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; K02-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; K02-1#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: D11-1#N.3, K03-1#N.5a, D11-1#N.14, K03-1#N.12, K03-1#N.16.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Fluid
items.clue: Any liquid or gas through which an object moves.

items.label: Free fall
items.clue: Motion in which gravity is the only force acting on the object.

items.label: Acceleration
items.clue: Gradient of a velocity–time graph; uniform when the line is straight.

items.label: Distance
items.clue: Whole area on a velocity–time graph with every part counted as positive.

questions.stem: A small steel ball is released from rest in air and falls until it reaches terminal velocity. How does its acceleration change during this time?

options.text: It is constant but less than g, because drag is constant.
It stays equal to g, since drag only lowers the ball's speed.
It increases, since the ball moves faster and faster as it falls.
It decreases from g towards zero as the drag increases.

questions.explanation: At release the ball is at rest, so there is no drag and its acceleration is g. As it speeds up the drag grows, so the acceleration decreases, reaching zero at terminal velocity.

questions.stem: A car travelling at 16 m s⁻¹ brakes with uniform deceleration and comes to rest in 4.0 s. What distance does the car travel while braking?

Two paper cones have the same size and shape. A second cone is pushed inside one of them, doubling its mass without changing its outside shape. Both are dropped from a high balcony. Which statement about their terminal velocities is correct?

options.text: Both reach the same terminal velocity, as all objects in free fall have the same acceleration.
The double cone reaches a higher terminal velocity, as drag must grow to equal a weight twice as large.
The double cone reaches a lower terminal velocity, as its greater weight gives it more drag at every speed.
The double cone reaches its terminal velocity sooner, as its greater weight gives it a greater acceleration from the start.

questions.stem: A student drops a ball from rest from several heights h and times each fall, t. She plots t² (y-axis) against h (x-axis): a straight line through the origin with gradient 0.204 s² m⁻¹. What value of g do the results give?
questions.explanation: h = ½gt² gives t² = (2/g)h, so the gradient is 2/g. g = 2 ÷ 0.204 = 9.80 m s⁻².

questions.stem: A toy car is released from rest on a straight slope and speeds up with constant acceleration. It travels 0.60 m in the first 2.0 s. How far does it travel between t = 4.0 s and t = 6.0 s?
